audios.title: An interview with a marine biologist
audios.instructions: Listen to the interview and choose the correct answer A, B, C or D.
audios.transcript: People often assume my passion for the ocean started because I grew up by the sea, but actually I lived in a city. My parents were not particularly interested in nature either. It was really a TV documentary I watched when I was about ten. It showed a coral reef in Australia and I was completely hooked. Climate change gets all the attention, and rising temperatures are certainly a huge problem, but in my opinion the most damaging factor is actually agricultural pollution. Overfishing is also a concern, but pollution is what is killing reefs fastest.

audios.title: Interview with an economist about remote work
audios.instructions: Listen to the interview and choose the correct answer A, B, C or D.
audios.transcript: So, Professor, is remote work here to stay? It is a complex question. The pandemic forced companies to try it, and many discovered that productivity did not fall. In fact, in some sectors it increased. However, we are now seeing a counter-trend. Some large companies are asking employees to return to the office, at least part of the week. Why is that? Several reasons. First, innovation often happens through spontaneous conversations in corridors. Second, there is a concern about company culture. New employees, in particular, struggle to learn from colleagues when they are working from home. What is the solution? I think the hybrid model is the most realistic. But it requires careful management. Companies need clear rules about when people should be in the office. Otherwise, you have the worst of both worlds - people who are neither fully connected to the office nor fully comfortable at home.

audios.title: Lecture about climate change
audios.instructions: Listen to the lecture and choose the correct answer A, B, C or D.
audios.transcript: Today I want to talk about the impact of climate change on agriculture. This is a topic that affects every one of us, because we all need to eat. Rising temperatures are already reducing crop yields in many parts of the world. In some regions, farmers are experiencing longer droughts, while in others they face devastating floods. According to recent studies, global food production could decline by up to 25 percent by 2050 if we do not take action. However, there is some good news. Scientists are developing new varieties of crops that can survive in hotter and drier conditions. Drip irrigation systems are helping farmers use water more efficiently. And in some countries, farmers are switching to traditional methods that have been used for centuries. The challenge is to make these solutions available and affordable for everyone, not just for wealthy nations.

audios.title: Interview with a neuroscientist about memory
audios.instructions: Listen to the interview and choose the correct answer A, B, C or D.
audios.transcript: Dr. Chen, is it true that our memory gets worse as we age? Well, that is a common belief, but it is not entirely accurate. Some types of memory do decline with age, particularly the ability to recall specific details quickly. But other aspects, like vocabulary and general knowledge, can actually improve until quite late in life. So why do older people forget things more often? It is not necessarily because their memory is worse. It is often because they have more information stored in their brains, so it takes longer to retrieve a specific memory. Think of it like a library. A small library is quick to search. A large library takes longer, but it has more books. That is a very useful image. What can we do to keep our memory sharp? Physical exercise is the single most effective thing. Sleep is also crucial. And learning new things, especially things that are challenging, keeps the brain active.

audios.title: Interview with a novelist about creativity
audios.instructions: Listen to the interview and choose the correct answer A, B, C or D.
audios.transcript: So, how do you write a novel? I get asked this a lot, and honestly, I don't have a magic formula. For me, it starts with a character, not a plot. I need to hear a voice in my head. Once I have that, I follow the character and see where they take me. Do you plan everything before you start? No, quite the opposite. I wish I could plan, but my brain doesn't work that way. I discover the story as I write it. That sounds chaotic. It is, at times. But it also means I am surprised by my own book. If I knew the ending before I started, I think I would lose interest. What advice would you give to young writers? Read. Read everything, not just the genre you want to write in. And write every day, even if it is only for fifteen minutes. The main thing is to finish something. A finished bad novel is worth more than an unfinished perfect one.

audios.title: Radio programme about urban planning
audios.instructions: Listen to the radio programme and choose the correct answer A, B, C or D.
audios.transcript: Welcome back to City Talk. Today we are discussing urban planning, and specifically the question of pedestrian zones. Many European cities have been closing their city centres to cars. Barcelona, for example, has created so-called superblocks, where cars are largely banned and streets are given back to pedestrians. Paris has reduced traffic along the Seine. The results have been impressive. Air pollution has fallen, noise levels have dropped, and local businesses in pedestrian areas often report higher sales because people walk more slowly and stop to look in shop windows. However, not everyone is happy. Some residents complain that it is now harder to reach essential services, especially for elderly people or those with disabilities. Delivery drivers also say their jobs have become much more difficult. The solution, according to urban planners, is to design these zones carefully - providing accessible public transport and exceptions for essential vehicles.

audios.title: Interview with a psychologist about stress
audios.instructions: Listen to the interview and choose the correct answer A, B, C or D.
audios.transcript: Dr. Patel, is stress always bad for us? Not at all. Stress is a natural response that helps us react to challenges. In small doses, it can actually improve performance. Think of athletes before a competition - they feel stressed, but that stress helps them focus. So, when does stress become a problem? When it becomes chronic. If the stress response is activated constantly, without time to recover, it damages our health. Chronic stress is linked to heart disease, depression, and a weakened immune system. What can people do about it? The key is recovery. Sleep is essential. Exercise helps. But the most important thing is social connection. Talking to a friend, spending time with family, even just being in the same room as someone you trust, reduces stress hormones. Interestingly, many people under stress do the opposite - they isolate themselves. That is exactly the wrong thing to do.

audios.title: Lecture about the history of the internet
audios.instructions: Listen to the lecture and choose the correct answer A, B, C or D.
audios.transcript: Today we are going to look at the history of the internet, which is more complex than most people realise. The origins of the internet go back to the 1960s, when the US Department of Defense funded a project called ARPANET. The goal was to create a communication network that could survive a nuclear attack. Messages could be sent through multiple routes, so if one route was destroyed, the message would still arrive. In the 1980s, the network expanded to include universities and research centres. But it was only in 1991 that the World Wide Web was created by Tim Berners-Lee, a British scientist working at CERN. The Web made the internet accessible to ordinary people. From that moment, the growth was explosive. Today, more than five billion people use the internet, and it has transformed almost every aspect of modern life. What is interesting is that no one owns the internet. It is a global network of networks, governed by shared protocols. That is both its greatest strength and its greatest weakness.
